mappings.note: Definition of an electric circuit. It is not Ohm's law and no circuit symbols are asked for, so it rests at the competency, which names the circuit and its characteristics.
Defines the ampere from charge per second. Ohm's law relates V, I and R but does not define the ampere, so competency level.
Names the cell as the device that maintains a potential difference; potential difference is one of the three quantities LO-1 relates.
Defines the volt as one joule per coulomb; potential difference, the first quantity in LO-1.
Energy per coulomb through a 6 V battery is a direct use of the potential-difference definition, so LO-1 rather than the appliance-energy outcome C 2.5-LO-1.
Asks the factors resistance depends on - length, area, material - which is verbatim LO-3.
Thick versus thin wire is resistance varying with area of cross-section; LO-3, not Ohm's law.
Stem is truncated and carries no antecedent, but it continues the thick/thin wire item, i.e. resistance against cross-section. Mapped on that.
Alloy rather than pure metal for toaster and iron coils: the element must produce heat and survive it. The heating-effect outcome, which names the heater explicitly.
Ranks conductors by resistivity values; the material clause of LO-3.
Equivalent resistance of two and of three resistors in parallel; the series/parallel outcome.
The cord stays cool while the element glows because heat depends on resistance; the heating-effect outcome.
Advantages of parallel over series for appliances; a property of the parallel combination.
Arranges 2, 3 and 6 ohms to reach 4 and 1 ohm; equivalent resistance in series and parallel.
The rate at which energy is delivered is electric power; the power outcome, not Ohm's law.
P = VI for the motor and then energy over 2 h; the power and energy outcome.
Two steps are both needed: cutting the wire into five parts divides the resistance by length (LO-3), and rejoining them in parallel divides it again (LO-2).
Picks the expression that is NOT a power formula; the power outcome.
Power at a non-rated voltage through P = V squared over R; the power outcome.
Heat ratio for the same two wires in series and in parallel: needs the equivalent resistance of each arrangement (LO-2) and Joule heating to compare (C 2.5-LO-2).
R = rho l / A solved for length, then the effect of doubling the diameter; the resistivity outcome.
Number of equal resistors in parallel to draw a stated current; equivalent resistance in parallel.
Least count of a voltmeter is instrument reading, which is the ammeter/voltmeter clause of C 8.1-LO-5.
Names the components of an Ohm's-law circuit; circuit-diagram outcome rather than the law itself.
Identifies the lettered components in a supplied circuit diagram; circuit-diagram outcome. Figure not stored.
Least counts of a voltmeter and an ammeter read off their scales; instrument-reading outcome. Figures not stored.
Which components of the drawn circuit are in series and which in parallel; reading a circuit diagram, so C 8.1-LO-5 rather than the equivalent-resistance outcome.
The key is removed so the wire does not heat, because Ohm's law only holds at constant temperature; that condition belongs to LO-1.
Zero-error correction on a milliammeter and a voltmeter; reading the instruments, the C 8.1-LO-5 clause.
Converts 17 scale divisions into amperes; instrument reading.
Precautions are about connecting and reading the meters correctly; circuit and instrument outcome.
Plots V against I and takes the resistance from the line; Ohm's law relating V, I and R.
Least count of an ammeter from range and divisions; instrument reading.
Classifies conductor and insulator from resistivity values; the material clause of LO-3.
The heating element is chosen purely on the resistivity figure supplied, so this is judged on LO-3 rather than on the heating effect itself.
Stem is only a lead-in - the resistivity table and the actual question are not stored - but it is plainly a resistivity-comparison item.
Chooses the heating-element material from tabulated resistivity; decided on LO-3, as with the companion item.
Labels V-I graphs as series or parallel by which combination has the larger resistance; the series/parallel outcome.
Compares two circuits for total resistance, current and whether the p.d. is shared; series versus parallel behaviour.
The fuse rating question needs the appliance current from P = VI (C 2.5-LO-1) and then the fuse's protective action (C 2.5-LO-2).
Reconciles P = I squared R with P = V squared / R; the power outcome.
Identifies the series-combination line among three V-I graphs by its larger resistance; series/parallel outcome.
Which wire produces more heat per unit time when joined to the same battery; Joule heating compared through resistance.
Stem is a lead-in only, with the table and the question itself missing, but it is a resistivity item.
Predicts which circuit gives the largest ammeter reading; literally the 'predicts the reading of an ammeter' clause of C 8.1-LO-5.
Compares power produced by different resistor arrangements on the same battery: needs the equivalent resistance (LO-2) and the power formula (C 2.5-LO-1).
Resistivity depends on the material alone, not on shape or size; the material clause of LO-3.
Number of electrons from I = Q/t and Q = ne. Charge-to-current arithmetic reaches no outcome, so competency level.
Picks the circuit whose components are properly connected; reading a circuit diagram.
Maximum resistance from five equal resistors is the series arrangement; equivalent resistance.
Minimum resistance from five equal resistors is the parallel arrangement; equivalent resistance.
Correct symbolic representation of cells in series for maximum potential; circuit-diagram outcome, not equivalent resistance.
Asks which expression represents voltage, i.e. V = IR or W/Q; the quantity LO-1 relates. Options are not stored with the stem.
Doubling the length and keeping R the same forces twice the area; R proportional to l/A, which is LO-3.
Orders three resistances from the slopes of their V-I lines; Ohm's law read off a graph.
Percentage rise in dissipated power when the current doubles, from P = I squared R; the power outcome.
Resistivity is unchanged by a change of shape; the material clause of LO-3.
Brightness of 40, 60 and 100 W bulbs at the same voltage is decided by their power ratings; the power outcome.
Heat in the 4 ohm resistor needs the series current (LO-2) and then H = I squared R t (C 2.5-LO-2).
Fuse rating for a 1 kW kettle: current from P = VI (C 2.5-LO-1), then the fuse choice (C 2.5-LO-2).
Which quantity is common in series and which in parallel for two unequal resistors; the series/parallel outcome.
Alternative units of electric power; the power outcome.
Corrects and redraws a faulty Ohm's-law circuit diagram; the circuit-diagram outcome.
Maximum current from a 18 W limit uses P = I squared R (C 2.5-LO-1) applied to the drawn combination (LO-2).
Why an ammeter must have low resistance; the ammeter clause of C 8.1-LO-5.
Explicitly asks for a drawn circuit with an ammeter and a voltmeter (C 8.1-LO-5) and then whether the p.d. is shared between a series resistor and a parallel block (LO-2).
How a fuse protects appliances; the fuse clause of C 2.5-LO-2.
Commercial unit of electrical energy expressed in joules; the kilowatt-hour clause of C 2.5-LO-1.
Lamp resistance from Ohm's law in a series circuit (LO-1), then the change when a 10 ohm branch is added in parallel (LO-2).
Why domestic wiring is parallel; a property of the parallel combination.
Predicts what each ammeter reads as bulbs fuse - the explicit ammeter-prediction clause of C 8.1-LO-5 - using the behaviour of the parallel network (LO-2).
Brightness and survival of bulbs in series versus parallel; the series/parallel outcome.
States Ohm's law, its verification and its limits; verbatim LO-1.
Defines resistivity with its unit and describes the experiment on the factors affecting resistance; verbatim LO-3.
Infers that the current is the same everywhere in a series circuit; a defining property of the series combination.
Infers that the p.d. is the same across parallel branches; a defining property of the parallel combination.
Joule's heating effect, its demonstration and four applications; verbatim C 2.5-LO-2.
Multi-part numerical: equivalent resistance and branch current for the combination (LO-2), then the dissipated power (C 2.5-LO-1).
Units saved per month by replacing bulbs with CFLs; energy consumed in kilowatt hours, verbatim C 2.5-LO-1.
A values-only item about switching off unused fans; it asks for no scientific reasoning at all, so it reaches no competency and sits at the goal.
The only assessable science part is the commercial unit of electrical energy; the kilowatt-hour clause of C 2.5-LO-1.
Defines electric potential; one of the three quantities LO-1 relates.
Relation V = W/q, the definition of potential difference.
SI unit of electric potential; potential difference in LO-1.
Defines one volt; potential difference in LO-1.
Whether potential is a scalar or a vector is a property of the quantity, not the V-I-R relation, so it rests at the competency.
Meaning of potential difference between two points; LO-1.
Names the voltmeter as the measuring instrument; the instrument clause of C 8.1-LO-5.
The potential difference is what keeps charge flowing; LO-1 relates it to current.
Defines electric current as charge per unit time; not the V-I-R relation, so competency level.
I = ne/t links current to the number of electrons; charge arithmetic, which no outcome covers.
SI unit of current; a definition rather than the Ohm's-law relation.
Defines one ampere from coulombs per second; no outcome defines the ampere.
Conventional current is opposite to electron flow; a convention about current, not the V-I-R relation.
Names the ammeter as the current-measuring instrument; the instrument clause of C 8.1-LO-5.
Ammeter is connected in series; the instrument-connection clause of C 8.1-LO-5.
Voltmeter is connected in parallel; the instrument-connection clause of C 8.1-LO-5.
Defines Ohm's law; verbatim the first clause of LO-1.
Draws the V-proportional-to-I conclusion from a graph; Ohm's law.
Formula linking I to V; Ohm's law.
Defines electrical resistance as V/I; the resistance term of Ohm's law.
SI unit of resistance; the resistance term of Ohm's law.
Defines one ohm as one volt producing one ampere - Ohm's law made into a definition.
Shape of the V-I graph for a conductor; the graphical form of Ohm's law.
The stem bundles two alternative questions: V/I is resistance (LO-1) and the quantity measured in volt-ampere is power (C 2.5-LO-1). Both are needed because the item can be set either way.
Slope of the V-I graph is the resistance; Ohm's law read graphically.
Effect of temperature on resistance. LO-3 names only length, area and material, so temperature reaches no outcome and this rests at the competency.
Decides which temperature gives the higher resistance from the slopes of two V-I lines; the resistance is read through Ohm's law, which is the assessable step.
Resistance against area of cross-section; verbatim LO-3.
R = rho l / A; verbatim LO-3.
Defines electrical resistivity; the material clause of LO-3.
SI unit of resistivity; LO-3.
Resistivity is unchanged when a wire is stretched; the material clause of LO-3.
Orders metal, alloy and insulator by resistivity; the material clause of LO-3.
Total of n equal resistors in series; equivalent resistance.
Connecting 6 and 3 ohm wires to obtain 2 ohms; equivalent resistance in parallel.
Explicitly asks for a drawn schematic with cells, resistors and a key; the circuit-diagram outcome.
Defines the heating effect of electric current; verbatim C 2.5-LO-2.
H = I squared R t; Joule's law, C 2.5-LO-2.
States Joule's law of heating; verbatim C 2.5-LO-2.
